title: Texas Push to Ban H-1B Teachers Draws Mounting Backlash From School Districts
excerpt: Governor Greg Abbott wants legislation ensuring “exactly zero” Texas public school employees hold H-1B visas; Dallas ISD, which sponsors 171, warns the ban would hollow out bilingual programs.
body:
• Governor Greg Abbott has proposed legislation to ensure "exactly zero" Texas public school employees are in the state on H-1B visas, as part of a broader push against foreign influence in education.
  • Texas schools employed 271 H-1B visa holders in 2025 — the most of any state — with Dallas ISD alone sponsoring 171, most of them bilingual and dual-language teachers.
  • School districts say they hire from abroad only to fill critical shortages identified by the Texas Education Agency, and warn the ban would hollow out bilingual programs.
  • The proposal requires legislation from the next legislative session; the Dallas Morning News editorial board has called the ban misguided.

Governor Greg Abbott's proposal to bar H-1B visa workers from Texas public schools is drawing mounting opposition from school districts and editorial boards, weeks after the governor pledged at a campaign stop that "exactly zero" public school employees should hold the federal visas.

The backlash crystallized in a recent Dallas Morning News editorial calling the proposed ban "misguided" and warning it could hollow out bilingual programs while doing little to address legitimate concerns about the visa program. Dallas ISD — which sponsors more H-1B employees than any school district in the country — has pushed back, saying it hires teachers from abroad only to fill critical shortages and that eliminating them would force the state to reckon with its teacher pipeline.

Context and Background

Abbott unveiled the proposal on August 18 at a campaign stop in Austin, where the Republican governor is running for reelection. Under the plan, Texas public schools would be prohibited from accepting gifts or entering into partnerships or financial arrangements with foreign governments and the entities they own, fund, or act through. Abbott said he will also seek legislation establishing a total ban on H-1B workers in Texas K-12 schools.

"We're tired of the federal government not putting limits on who can come in under H-1Bs, and because of the federal government's failure to control H-1B visas, Texas is having to put our foot down, and that means making some tough decisions," Abbott said when announcing the proposals.

The proposal extends a campaign Abbott began in January, when he ordered all public universities and state agencies to freeze new H-1B visa petitions without written permission from the Texas Workforce Commission — a freeze that remains in effect through the end of the next legislative session on May 31, 2027. Abbott referenced President Trump's September 2025 proclamation stating the visa program was intended to supplement the U.S. workforce rather than replace American workers.

How Schools Use the Visas

Universities and related health institutions employ the majority of H-1B holders in Texas education, but several school districts rely on the visas to fill hard-to-staff roles. Texas schools employed 271 H-1B visa holders in 2025, more than any other state, according to an analysis by the National Education Association. The state's public schools employ more than 320,000 teachers overall.

Dallas ISD sponsors 171 visa holders — more than any district or public university in Texas — between July 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026, according to federal data, covering new applications and renewals. Of those, 73% are teachers in the dual-language program, in a district serving about 56,000 students learning English and enrolled in bilingual or English-as-a-second-language programs.

"We only hire teachers from abroad to fill critical shortages identified by the Texas Education Agency, and each of these teachers is certified by the TEA as well. If the governor's new expectation is to eliminate these teachers, then we're going to need more Texans in the teaching pipeline."

— Dallas ISD, in a statement

Education Week noted that the move, if approved, would eliminate a staffing strategy districts use to fill hard-to-staff teaching roles in subjects like math and foreign languages — and that Texas' influence could inspire similar discussions in other states.

Impact and Analysis

The Dallas Morning News editorial argued that an outright ban calling for "exactly zero" H-1B employees goes too far. Native speakers bring fluency and cultural experience especially valuable in foreign language and dual-language classrooms, it said — and removing them because of immigration status would narrow the pool of talented teachers. The paper noted that schools have abused H-1B visas in the past, citing a Garland district administrator in the early 2000s who illegally recruited teachers and profited from their employment, but argued that evidence of abuse should trigger investigations, not a blanket ban.

Abbott has said the law would apply to both current H-1B holders and future applicants, which means hundreds of teachers and staff could lose their jobs if it passes. The Legislature, which convenes next year, must approve the change before the governor can sign it. If successful, Texas would become the first state to block school districts from hiring H-1B visa holders.

Diaspora Angle

Indian professionals form a large share of H-1B holders in Texas — home to one of the biggest Indian-American communities in the country, concentrated in Dallas, Houston, and Austin — and Indian teachers are among those recruited for bilingual and specialized classroom roles. A ban that forces current visa holders out of their jobs would hit Indian families in Texas directly, and the governor's broader "foreign influence" framing has unsettled parents who view international teachers as an asset rather than a risk.

What's Next

The proposal remains just that — a proposal. Abbott must shepherd legislation through a session that does not begin until next year, and the opposition from the state's second-largest district gives skeptical lawmakers cover to push back. Watch whether other large districts, charter networks, and teacher groups join Dallas ISD publicly, and whether Abbott expands the freeze he imposed on universities in January to K-12 hiring before the session.
